prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B001 alone, Katori and Ye. The chair asks what is new relative to 2005 and 2012. The 2005 prize gave the field the frequency comb, a way to count optical cycles. The 2012 prize honoured control and measurement of individual quantum systems, which includes single-ion clocks. A single ion gives an excellent reference but very little signal, so averaging time is the limit. The lattice clock answers a different problem: it interrogates thousands of atoms at once while a magic wavelength makes the trap light shift the two clock levels equally, so confinement does not broaden or move the line. That is a design principle, not a refinement of a comb or an ion trap, and it is what opened the regime of many-atom coherence, density-dependent shifts and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength idea and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group carried it to the 1e-18 level and into many-body physics. The performance is verified by clock-to-clock comparison, which is the strongest kind of confirmation an experimentalist can ask for. No hard exclusion is forced by the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: Distinctness is still the real vulnerability. A committee that counts prizes by lineage will say that frequency metrology has been honoured in 2005 and 2012 and that lattice clocks are the third prize in about twenty-five years. I think that confuses lineage with discovery, but I cannot dismiss it, and my own training in Hall's laboratory is the reason I try to test the objection harder than I otherwise would. The citation must be worded around the magic-wavelength lattice and not around optical frequency metrology in general. Priority outside the two names remains open: Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and Paris groups contributed to the early lattice-clock record. From memory, Katori's proposal came before the first experiments, but I have not verified the chronology against primary sources and the chair's question on this has no better answer from me than that. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so part of the consequence is prospective.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B001 but states the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is in lineage rather than discovery, and disagrees with my second-place opening choice of B046 because the Cirac-Zoller-Blatt prize would overlap with 2012 more directly than the lattice clock does.
responses.response: I accept the criticism of B046 and it is not part of my preferred configuration. Trapped-ion quantum computation sits closer to the 2012 prize than the lattice clock does, and my familiarity with quantum-information work in atoms is a reason to discount my enthusiasm for it, as I noted in round 1. Your distinction between lineage and discovery is the one I rely on for B001, and I would write the citation so that the new element, many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, is stated explicitly and the comb and single-ion work are not claimed. I also agree with your position that the redefinition of the second is a consequence and not a precondition.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B013 as his first choice because the conceptual break is sharper than for precision metrology, accepts B001 as a strong alternative, and asks that the third precision-frequency prize in twenty-five years be weighed.
responses.response: I take the novelty argument seriously and it is why B013 is my first alternative. Two things keep me with B001. First, on robustness: the clock accuracy is an observable that independent laboratories check against each other, whereas the twisted-bilayer record still has open questions on pairing, twist-angle disorder and device-to-device variation. Second, on novelty, I do not think the third-prize count is the right measure, because the magic-wavelength lattice is a new way to build a measurement and not a further turn of the earlier ones. I concede your point on Andrei: a three-person limit forces an exclusion with a real claim behind it, and that is a cost the clock prize does not carry. If the committee settles that cost openly, B013 becomes a close competitor for me.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B013 but says that if maturity is weighted over novelty then B001 is the safer pick, and wants any citation to rest on flat bands and the correlated phases rather than on the pairing mechanism.
responses.response: I agree with your own conditional and I weigh maturity more heavily than novelty here, since a prize should honour what no longer depends on interpretation. I also agree that a B013 citation resting on the flat-band prediction and the correlated and superconducting phases, and not on the pairing mechanism, would be defensible, and that this answers part of the maturity objection. It does not answer it fully, because the committee would still be honouring a platform whose phase diagram is moving. The Bistritzer-MacDonald pair is the stronger argument for B013, and I agree with you against Pearce that splitting that theory credit is harder to defend than naming Andrei in the committee discussion.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the polarisabilities and blackbody and relativistic shifts make the systematics hard physics, and says she would support B013 as a second choice and B024 only if the HgTe prediction can be separated from Kane-Mele and Molenkamp.
responses.response: The systematic-shift budget is the part that persuades me most as an experimentalist, because a claimed 1e-18 is only a result once those shifts are bounded and checked against a second clock. On B024 I share your difficulty: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp tested, so I do not yet see how it is separated from the trio, and I would not move B024 above B013 until it is. On the chair's second question, I have not checked the priority chronology for the other lattice-clock groups against primary sources and neither of us should claim more than we know, but nothing I recall suggests that Katori and Ye are not the two decisive names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or will count it as a third precision-frequency prize.
The priority chronology among Katori, Ye and the other early lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto, PTB, NIST, Paris), which I recall only from general knowledge and have not verified.
Whether B013 would overtake B001 for the committee if the Andrei question and the maturity question are settled in its favour.
Whether the topological-insulator credit can be scoped to a defensible three-name cut, which would affect how serious an alternative B024 is.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory during my doctoral period. Hall is not a candidate, but his 2005 prize is the closest prior-prize lineage to B001, so I disclose it as a connection that could bear on how I judge distinctness, and I have tried to apply the distinctness objection at least as strictly as others. I have no documented relationship with Katori or Ye. My Lund atomic-physics and quantum-memory work is adjacent to B041 and B046, and I discount my enthusiasm for them. No other specific conflict is apparent.
